report.source_text: Results showed two pathogenic variants in the KCNJ1 gene [1]: a paternally inherited frameshift deletion, p.Glu334Glyfs*35 (c.996_999del, exon 5), predicted to result in premature protein termination and previously reported as causative for Bartter syndrome [6], and [2] a maternally inherited missense variant, p. Pro110Leu (c.329C > T, exon 5) (Fig. 2), previously reported to be pathogenic in compound heterozygosity with other pathogenic variants in KCNJ1 [8–10].

report.source_text: The patient required sodium chloride supplementation up to a maximum dose of 7.9 mmol/kg/day included in the total parenteral nutrition, started on day of life 7 to gradually achieve normal sodium levels. A trial of fludrocortisone therapy was recommended by endocrinology to definitively rule out CAH. The patient received two doses given on day 9 (0.03 mg/kg/dose) of life and was without clinical response. The patient’s electrolytes normalized by 4 weeks of life and supplementation was gradually weaned off by 7 weeks of life.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Bartter syndrome type II with compound heterozygosity for pathogenic KCNJ1 gene variants
clinician.trajectory_summary: A premature female infant born at 33+6 weeks with antenatal polyhydramnios presented with poor responsiveness, clinical dehydration, and required non-invasive ventilation. Early workup revealed hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and low chloride levels in the first week alongside high urinary sodium indicating renal salt wasting. Genetic testing confirmed two pathogenic KCNJ1 variants in compound heterozygosity, consistent with Bartter syndrome type II. Treatment with sodium supplementation normalized electrolytes by 4 weeks, with weaning by 7 weeks and no response to fludrocortisone trial. Follow-up at 6 months showed normal electrolytes, confirming resolution of hyponatremia and absence of classic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis on follow-up.
